mu-37f691b4.stem: After a difficult vaginal delivery a patient with incontinence of flatus and faeces is found to have a tear of the anal sphincter complex. Which nerve supplies the voluntarily controlled external anal sphincter?
mu-37f691b4.explanation: The external anal sphincter is striated muscle supplied by the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve; a difficult delivery can cause both a muscle tear and stretch injury of the pudendal nerve. The internal sphincter is smooth muscle controlled by autonomic nerves (sympathetic: contraction).
notes: It supplies the cremaster and the skin of the upper front of the thigh.
It supplies the adductor muscles of the thigh.
They are parasympathetic; they relax the internal sphincter.
It is sympathetic; it contracts the internal sphincter.

mu-d7d1a44a.stem: Which rotator cuff muscles are supplied by the suprascapular nerve?
mu-d7d1a44a.explanation: The suprascapular nerve passes through the suprascapular notch to supply supraspinatus, then winds around the spinoglenoid notch to supply infraspinatus. Teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve and subscapularis by the subscapular nerves; teres major is not part of the rotator cuff.

mu-88287625.stem: A 62-year-old with shoulder pain has the arm passively abducted to 90° and released; he cannot lower it slowly and it drops suddenly. What is the most likely tear?
mu-88287625.explanation: The drop-arm test indicates a supraspinatus tear; this tendon is the rotator cuff tendon most exposed to impingement and degeneration in the narrow space under the acromion. In subscapularis tears the lift-off and belly-press tests are abnormal; in teres minor tears external rotation strength is impaired.

mu-d031ad64.stem: Which structure passes through the triangular space (between teres minor, teres major and the long head of triceps)?
options: Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
mu-d031ad64.explanation: The triangular space contains only the circumflex scapular artery, which joins the anastomotic network behind the scapula. The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery pass through the quadrangular space, the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery through the triangular interval between triceps and teres major.
notes: It accompanies latissimus dorsi; it does not pass through this space.
They pass through the quadrangular space.
It passes through the suprascapular notch.
They pass through the triangular interval below teres major.

mu-ef88590d.stem: Which structures pass through the triangular interval between the lower border of teres major and the long and lateral heads of triceps?
options: Ulnar nerve and superior ulnar collateral artery
Axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery
Radial nerve and profunda brachii artery
mu-ef88590d.explanation: The radial nerve passes from the axilla to the back of the arm through this interval and reaches the radial groove of the humerus with the profunda brachii artery; it is injured here in fractures of the humeral shaft.

options: Lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus
mu-61cd53db.explanation: Deltoid arises from the lateral third of the clavicle, the acromion and the spine of the scapula and inserts into the deltoid tuberosity on the lateral surface of the humeral shaft. It is the main muscle of abduction of the arm between 15° and 90°; it is supplied by the axillary nerve.

mu-b9e6a413.stem: Where does the short head of biceps brachii arise?
options: From the tip of the coracoid process
mu-b9e6a413.explanation: The short head arises from the coracoid process by a common tendon with coracobrachialis; the long head arises from the supraglenoid tubercle and glenoid labrum, and its tendon runs through the joint capsule down into the intertubercular sulcus.
notes: This is the origin of the long head of triceps.
This is the origin of deltoid.
This is the origin of the long head.
This is the insertion of subscapularis.

mu-c4396e46.stem: Which statement about the bicipital aponeurosis (lacertus fibrosus) is true?
options: It covers the brachial artery and median nerve in the cubital fossa
It is the tendon of brachialis
It forms the floor of the cubital fossa
It attaches to the radial tuberosity
mu-c4396e46.explanation: The aponeurosis passing medially from the biceps tendon blends with the deep fascia of the forearm; it covers the brachial artery and median nerve and lies beneath the median cubital vein. So in venous procedures it protects the structures beneath it.
notes: The radial nerve lies on the lateral side of the cubital fossa, between brachioradialis and brachialis.
It separates from biceps brachii.
The floor is formed by brachialis and supinator.
The biceps tendon attaches to the radial tuberosity.

options: Middle of the lateral surface of the radial shaft
Base of the radial styloid process
mu-a9fce112.explanation: Brachioradialis arises from the lateral supracondylar ridge and inserts into the lower end of the radius. It flexes the elbow with the forearm half-pronated; it is an elbow flexor supplied by the radial nerve. Pronator teres inserts into the middle of the radial shaft.

mu-11f202e1.stem: From where do the superficial flexor muscles of the forearm arise by a common tendon?
mu-11f202e1.explanation: Pronator teres, flexor carpi radialis, palmaris longus, flexor digitorum superficialis and flexor carpi ulnaris arise by the common flexor tendon from the medial epicondyle. Overloading this tendon causes medial epicondylitis (golfer's elbow); the extensors arise from the lateral epicondyle.

mu-501c4de2.stem: Which quadrilateral muscle lies distally in the deepest layer of the anterior forearm?
mu-501c4de2.explanation: Pronator quadratus runs between the anterior surfaces of the distal quarters of the ulna and radius; it is the main muscle initiating pronation and holds the distal radio-ulnar joint together. It is supplied by the anterior interosseous nerve.

mu-6ac03b3c.stem: Which nerve is compressed in the supinator canal (arcade of Frohse), and what is the typical finding?
options: Median nerve – thenar wasting and ape hand
Anterior interosseous nerve – inability to make the 'OK' sign
Posterior interosseous nerve – loss of finger extension with sensation preserved
Superficial branch of the radial nerve – sensory loss on the back of the hand only
mu-6ac03b3c.explanation: The deep branch of the radial nerve can be compressed as it passes between the two heads of supinator (arcade of Frohse). Because it is a motor branch, the fingers cannot be extended at the MCP joints, but there is no sensory loss. The branches to ECRL and brachioradialis arise higher, so wrist extension is preserved and deviates radially.

mu-e76c286d.stem: Where does the palmaris longus tendon pass at the wrist?
options: In front of the flexor retinaculum (outside the carpal tunnel)
mu-e76c286d.explanation: The palmaris longus tendon passes in front of the retinaculum and continues into the palmar aponeurosis; it is absent in 10–15% of people and is often used for tendon grafts. It is felt in the middle of the wrist, just in front of the median nerve.

mu-cab81e1d.stem: Which tendons lie in the 1st extensor compartment on the dorsum of the wrist?
options: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis
Abductor pollicis longus and extensor pollicis brevis
mu-cab81e1d.explanation: The compartments beneath the extensor retinaculum, from radial to ulnar: 1) APL–EPB, 2) ECRL–ECRB, 3) EPL, 4) ED–EI, 5) EDM, 6) ECU. Tenosynovitis of the first compartment is De Quervain's disease.
notes: They are in the 4th compartment.
They are in the 2nd compartment.
It is in the 3rd compartment.
It is in the 6th compartment.
